tools.name: Skill
tools.description:
Invoke a skill.

A skill is a packaged set of instructions the user or project has set up for a particular kind of task (deploy steps, a review checklist, a repo-specific workflow). Available skills appear in a system-reminder listing with one-line descriptions. When the task at hand is one a listed skill covers, call this tool first — the skill's instructions load into the turn for you to follow in place of your default approach; some skills instead run in a subagent and return the finished result. A skill that runs in the background returns only the agent's name — its result arrives later as a task notification, so don't wait on it or invoke it again in the meantime. Users may also ask for one by name (`/<name>`, or "slash command"); that's a request to invoke it.

- `skill`: exact name from the listing, no leading slash. Plugin skills use `plugin:skill`. Directory-scoped skills are listed with a path prefix (`apps/web:deploy`); when both scoped and unscoped variants of a name exist, pick the one whose directory contains the files you're working on (most specific wins; unscoped otherwise).
- `args`: optional arguments to pass through.

Only names from the listing (or that the user typed explicitly) are valid. Built-in CLI commands (`/help`, `/clear`, …) aren't skills. If a `<command-name>` block is already present this turn, the skill is loaded — follow it directly rather than calling again.

Execute a workflow script that orchestrates multiple subagents deterministically. Workflows run in the background — this tool returns immediately with a task ID, and a <task-notification> arrives when the workflow completes. Use /workflows to watch live progress.

ONLY call this tool when the user has explicitly opted into multi-agent orchestration. Workflows can spawn dozens of agents and consume a large amount of tokens; the user must request that scale, not have it inferred. Explicit opt-in means one of:
- The user included the keyword "ultracode" in their prompt (you'll see a system-reminder confirming it).
- Ultracode is on for the session (a system-reminder confirms it) — see **Ultracode** in the workflow authoring reference.
- The user directly asked you to run a workflow or use multi-agent orchestration in their own words ("use a workflow", "run a workflow", "fan out agents", "orchestrate this with subagents"). The ask must be in the user's words — a task that would merely benefit from a workflow does not count.
- The user invoked a skill or slash command whose instructions tell you to call Workflow.
- The user asked you to run a specific named or saved workflow.

For any other task — even one that would clearly benefit from parallelism — do NOT call this tool. Use the Agent tool (if available) for individual subagents, or briefly describe what a multi-agent workflow could do and how much it would roughly cost, and ask the user whether to run it. Mention they can ask for one with "use a workflow" in a future message to skip the ask.

Every script must begin with `export const meta = {...}`: a PURE LITERAL (no variables, calls or interpolation) giving the workflow's `name`, a one-line `description` (shown in the permission dialog) and optionally `phases` — one `{ title, detail? }` per phase() call, titles matched exactly. Pass the script inline via `script` — do not Write it to a file first, and do not also set the tool's `name` input (that selects a saved workflow); it is plain JavaScript, not TypeScript.

The canonical multi-stage pattern — pipeline by default, each dimension verifies as soon as its review completes:
  export const meta = {
    name: 'review-changes',
    description: 'Review changed files across dimensions, verify each finding',
    phases: [{ title: 'Review' }, { title: 'Verify' }],
  }
  const DIMENSIONS = [{key: 'bugs', prompt: '...'}, {key: 'perf', prompt: '...'}]
  const results = await pipeline(
    DIMENSIONS,
    d => agent(d.prompt, {label: `review:${d.key}`, phase: 'Review', schema: FINDINGS_SCHEMA}),
    review => parallel(review.findings.map(f => () =>
      agent(`Adversarially verify: ${f.title}`, {label: `verify:${f.file}`, phase: 'Verify', schema: VERDICT_SCHEMA})
        .then(v => ({...f, verdict: v}))
    ))
  )
  const confirmed = results.flat().filter(Boolean).filter(f => f.verdict?.isReal)
  return { confirmed }
  // Dimension 'bugs' findings verify while dimension 'perf' is still reviewing. No wasted wall-clock.

## Next

Ranked by real use: Skill-tool calls and typed `/commands` in the last 60 days of session logs, owned skills only (`skill-audit-next.py`). First five picked 2026-10-30.

| # | Skill | Runs (60 d) | Why it is on the list | Care |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | `forecast-capture` | 12 | Weekly in-season Big 12 forecast freeze. | Mid-season: audit on a non-Wednesday, and change nothing that alters a capture already made. |
| 2 | `project` | 6 | The portfolio registry and board; weekly-review's sweep reads the same registry. | `portfolio.json` has write-provenance rules (Tier A `portfolio-registry-write-provenance`). |
| 3 | `codex-review` | 4 | Codex reviews a plan in a bounded loop; the audit Method calls `codex exec` directly, not this skill. | Overlaps `claudex-loop` mode=review: check which one Eric actually runs before fixing both. |
| 4 | `ingest-book` | 2 | Turns a whole book into vault notes; the costliest atomization run. | Tier A `ingest-review-gate`: Eric reviews before any costly run. Test on a short source, never a full book unasked. |
| 5 | `name-meetings` | 2 | Renames Fireflies meetings with generic titles; meeting-sync calls it. | Renames go to the Fireflies API (outside service): test the detect step only; applying renames waits for Eric. |

When the script prints nothing, every used skill has been audited: tell Eric, and keep **Next** shorter than five.

## Method

What "audit like we've been doing" means, in order:

1. **Load** `mattpocock-skills:writing-for-agents` through the Skill tool (see Rules).
2. **Read** the skill, its other files, and the scripts and CLIs it calls. Find its callers (`grep -rn '<name>' ~/.claude/skills/*/SKILL.md`) and any scheduled job that does the same work.
3. **Verify every claim** against the real thing: paths exist, `--help` matches the flags, error codes and log lines exist in the script, the schedule matches the plist. Look at recent real runs (logs, outputs) for what actually went wrong.
4. **Fix**: real bugs first, then the writing-for-agents pass (steps in run order, a **Done when** line, positive rules, one home per fact, reference only some runs need moved to a sibling file). A script fix that adds a branch gets a small test.
5. **Test** by running the skill for real where it is safe. Data sent to an outside service (Jev, email, Teams) waits for Eric.
6. **Codex review**: `codex exec -s read-only "<prompt>" < /dev/null` on the diff (without `< /dev/null` it can wait on stdin forever), output to `~/.claude/audits/codex-review-<topic>-<date>.{md,txt}`. Check each finding before fixing it.
7. **Close**: portability check (`python3 ~/DEV/KeystoneOS/scripts/skill-portability-check.py`), commit by path in each repo touched, push, and add a line to `~/DEV/docs/STATUS.md` (and the touched repo's own STATUS).

| 2026-10-30 | `weekly-review` | skills `db60b87`, `8e0ea63`, `fe6b76b` | No `python` on the Mac; `--agent` emptied Fireflies rows; one ask with picks. |
| 2026-10-30 | `backup` | skills `ab87c9d`, `3d15e0d`, `fe6b76b`; dotclaude `d6ab8bc`, `8fcfb93` | Stale 21:00 schedule; a dry run could hide a failed day. |

ignores `argument-hint` / `allowed-tools`. Codex over-fires without the negative clause;

   it is also how the cut reaches Windows.** Undo with

   (`skills-archive/` is not in the repo and never reaches the other machine).

   98 of the 99 archived skills were still live in the pool (306 entries there vs 61
   canonical). Claude Code stopped seeing them; **Pi auto-discovers that folder**, so
   installing Pi would have re-exposed all of them. Always cut both.
3. **Skills live in three places and it is easy to edit the wrong copy.**
   `~/.claude/skills/` (19 entries were symlinks pointing *out* to the pool),
   `~/.agents/skills/` (Pi, Cowork), `~/.codex/skills/` (Codex, 27 symlinks + 5 real
   dirs). Count with `find -L`; plain `find` undercounts.
4. **`sync-to-codex.sh` did `rm -rf "$dst/$s"; cp -R "$SRC/$s"`** over a 7-name
   allowlist. If `$SRC/$s` ever became a symlink into `$dst`, that deletes the real
   data. `dev-sync` tells you to run it after every pull. A `.ps1` twin has the same
   shape — patch both.
5. **`~/.claude/skills/_shared/`** holds `config.json` + `Inference/` and is resolved by
   10+ skills via `parents[2]/_shared/config.json`. It has **no SKILL.md**. Never treat
   "no SKILL.md" as "orphan, delete".
6. **"606 plugin skills" is cache, not load.** Only 6 of 24 plugins are enabled
   (~37 skills exposed). The rest are disabled plugins and old cached versions.

## Executed 2026-09-12 — traps the live run found

- **Views are live links now.** `~/.agents/skills/<owned>` and `~/.codex/skills/<owned>`
  point into canonical, so anything that writes a view path writes canonical
  (`graphify install --platform agents` does; see [[graphify-runtime-setup]]).

  ignore that file, so an owned skill set `"off"` there is hidden in Claude Code but live
  elsewhere. Perfect frontmatter does not help; `skill-portability-check.py` fails it.
  Resolved 2026-09-13: Eric re-enabled the 7 (ArXiv, ISA, Science, capture-insight,
  library-review, pp-espn, session-miner) — `~/.claude` commit `21c686d`, checker 42/42.
  Never set an owned skill "off" again; retire it from canonical instead.

content.text:
Base directory for this skill: /Users/kristinarash/.claude/skills/memory-write

# Memory Write

Two branches: **Write** (add, replace, remove a fact) and **Recall** (answer from past context). Take the one the request needs.

## Tiers

Ask: "Will this fact still be true and useful in 3 months, across projects?" Yes → Tier A. Work in play now → Tier B.

**Tier A: `~/.claude/projects/<slug>/memory/`**, one file per fact, indexed by that folder's `MEMORY.md`.

| Fact | File | `metadata.type` |
|---|---|---|
| Durable user fact | `user_<name>.md` | `user` |
| Stable project convention or gotcha | `project_<name>.md` | `project` |
| Behavior rule from Eric | `feedback_<name>.md` | `feedback` |
| Pointer to an outside system | `reference_<name>.md` | `reference` |

- **Slug**: use the memory folder the harness names in this session's system prompt. It is the absolute cwd with every non-letter, non-digit folded to `-` (`~/DEV/CLI_Dev` → `-Users-kristinarash-DEV-CLI-Dev`).
- **Machine**: write to this machine's slug (Mac: `-Users-kristinarash-*`). The other machine never auto-injects it. Durable project facts belong in the repo's `docs/`, which both machines and the cloud see.
- **`name:`** is the filename stem minus its leading type token, kebab-cased: `feedback_project_idea_capture.md` → `project-idea-capture`. `[[links]]` target this bare name. (A 2026-09-02 audit found the corpus split 59 bare / 58 prefixed, which broke 37 links. `remember.py` enforces the rule.)

**Tier B: `~/.claude/global-memory/`**, two capped files. Caps are in characters, and only this skill enforces them: the SessionStart hook (`~/.claude/hooks/keystone-unified-snapshot.js`) injects both files whole.

| Fact | Home | Cap |
|---|---|---|
| In-progress work | `MEMORY.md` `## Active Threads` (max 5; park one to add one) | 2,500 |
| Paused work | `MEMORY.md` `## Parked` | (same file) |
| Current env notes | `MEMORY.md` `## Environment Notes` | (same file) |
| Decisions waiting on Eric | `MEMORY.md` `## Pending Decisions` | (same file) |
| Durable user profile | `USER.md` | 1,375 |

USER.md holds only the profile lines every session needs. Detail about Eric goes to a Tier A `user_` file.

## Write

1. **Pick the tier** with the tables above.
2. **Dedup.** Tier A: grep the slug's folder for the fact's key words (`grep -ril '<word>' <memory folder>`) and read every hit. `remember.py` checks only names, not content. Tier B: read the target file in full. If the fact exists, replace it in place; that is the default over adding.
3. **Write it.**
   - **Tier A add or replace**, one call, run from the project folder (`--dir <memory folder>` overrides):
     `python3 ~/.claude/scripts/remember.py --type <t> --name <bare-name> --desc "<one line>" --hook "<when to open>" [--why "..." --how "..."] "<fact>"`
     It writes the file and the index line, reads both back, and refreshes recall.py's index. Exit 0 prints `PASS`. Exit 2 means the name exists or looks alike: read that file, then rerun with `--type <its type> --name <its name> --update`, or add `--force` for a genuinely new fact. Exit 1 is a `FAIL`; fix the input it names.
   - **Tier A replace of a legacy file** (underscores after the type, like `project_kenny_boyd.md`; ~40 exist): `remember.py` would write a second file. Edit the old file in place and keep its index line.
   - **Tier B**: measure first, `python3 -c "import sys;print(len(open(sys.argv[1]).read()))" ~/.claude/global-memory/MEMORY.md` (or `USER.md`). If the write would pass the cap, merge or prune stale lines first. Then edit under the right `##` section.
   - **Remove (either tier)**: ask Eric first. Tier A: delete the file and its line in the slug's `MEMORY.md`; recall.py drops the file on its next run. Tier B: delete the line.
4. **Verify.**
   - Tier A: `remember.py`'s `PASS` covers read-back, the `name`/`description`/`type` frontmatter lines, and one index pointer. After a hand edit, check those three yourself.
   - Tier B: read the file back. The fact appears once, in the intended section, and the character count is at or under the cap.
   - Both: read the surrounding section for a contradiction or stale twin, and resolve it.
5. **Confirm** in one line: `Saved — will be active from next session.`

**Done when** the fact is in one home, every check in step 4 passed, and the confirmation is sent. On a failed check, report `FAIL`, the path, and the check instead of the confirmation.

USER.md and MEMORY.md are a frozen snapshot, injected once at session start to keep the prompt cache. A write persists now and is active next session; the one-line confirmation is the whole announcement.

## Recall

Climb in order. Stop as soon as the question is answered.

1. **Tier 0**: what is already in context: USER.md, MEMORY.md, and this folder's Tier A index. Zero cost.
2. **L1**: `python3 ~/.claude/scripts/recall.py "question"`. Plain code, ~1 s: keyword rank over the memsearch roots, the whole vault, and every `projects/*/memory` folder. It opens the best file and prints the matching paragraphs; on a weak match it also runs memsearch (~10 s). If the paragraphs miss, open the #2 or #3 candidate it lists.
3. **L2**: `python3 ~/.claude/scripts/recall.py "<reworded question>" --deep`. Always adds memsearch's hybrid meaning search (~10 s), memory files first.
4. **L3**: `memsearch expand <chunk_hash>`: the full section around a hit.
5. **L4**: `memsearch transcript <session_id>`: raw dialogue. Last resort.
6. **Fallback**: "I don't have a record of that."

The daily compiled logs (`~/.claude/claude-memory-compiler/daily/<YYYY-MM-DD>.md`) arrive as a pointer, not content. Open one when the question names that day. Only `claude-memory-compiler` writes them.

**A wrong or stale recall becomes a bench question, unasked.** When Eric corrects a recalled fact, or a newer file proves your recalled answer stale, in the same session:

1. Add one row to `~/.claude/scripts/recall-bench/questions.tsv`: `miss`, the question as asked, the file holding the right answer, the right answer in one line (tab-separated).
2. Run `CSET=miss bash ~/.claude/scripts/recall-bench/run.sh C` (~Remember:.06 a question) and note the result in that folder's `results.md`.
3. Run `python3 -I ~/.claude/scripts/recall-bench/check.py`. When it prints `OK`, run it again with `--update-baseline`. The daily backup's check guards each question that was a hit in `baseline.json`, so the new question is guarded only after this update, and only once recall.py ranks it first. On a `DROP`, report it and leave the baseline alone.
4. Tell Eric in one line.

# Skill audit list

"The list" for skill audits. When Eric says "audit the next skill on the list", take the first row under **Next** and follow **Method**.

**Rules (Eric, 2026-10-30):**

- **Next always holds five.** When a skill's audit is done, in the same commit as the fix: move its row to **Done** (date, commits, headline), then refill **Next** with the top skill from `python3 ~/.claude/scripts/skill-audit-next.py` as the new last row (runs, why, care).
- **Done is final.** A skill in **Done** never returns to **Next**, unless Eric explicitly names it to be added back. Then move its row back to **Next** and note the date he asked. The script already skips every skill in either table.
- **Every audit runs `mattpocock-skills:writing-for-agents`.** Call it through the Skill tool at the start of each audit, and again for the review pass, even when it ran earlier in the session. Working from memory of it is the slip this rule exists for (the 10-30 meeting-sync audit missed six wording faults until the skill was called).

## Next

Ranked by real use: Skill-tool calls and typed `/commands` in the last 60 days of session logs, owned skills only (`skill-audit-next.py`). First five picked 2026-10-30.

| # | Skill | Runs (60 d) | Why it is on the list | Care |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | `forecast-capture` | 12 | Weekly in-season Big 12 forecast freeze. | Mid-season: audit on a non-Wednesday, and change nothing that alters a capture already made. |
| 2 | `project` | 6 | The portfolio registry and board; weekly-review's sweep reads the same registry. | `portfolio.json` has write-provenance rules (Tier A `portfolio-registry-write-provenance`). |
| 3 | `codex-review` | 4 | Codex reviews a plan in a bounded loop; the audit Method calls `codex exec` directly, not this skill. | Overlaps `claudex-loop` mode=review: check which one Eric actually runs before fixing both. |
| 4 | `ingest-book` | 2 | Turns a whole book into vault notes; the costliest atomization run. | Tier A `ingest-review-gate`: Eric reviews before any costly run. Test on a short source, never a full book unasked. |
| 5 | `name-meetings` | 2 | Renames Fireflies meetings with generic titles; meeting-sync calls it. | Renames go to the Fireflies API (outside service): test the detect step only; applying renames waits for Eric. |

When the script prints nothing, every used skill has been audited: tell Eric, and keep **Next** shorter than five.

## Method

What "audit like we've been doing" means, in order:

1. **Load** `mattpocock-skills:writing-for-agents` through the Skill tool (see Rules).
2. **Read** the skill, its other files, and the scripts and CLIs it calls. Find its callers (`grep -rn '<name>' ~/.claude/skills/*/SKILL.md`) and any scheduled job that does the same work.
3. **Verify every claim** against the real thing: paths exist, `--help` matches the flags, error codes and log lines exist in the script, the schedule matches the plist. Look at recent real runs (logs, outputs) for what actually went wrong.
4. **Fix**: real bugs first, then the writing-for-agents pass (steps in run order, a **Done when** line, positive rules, one home per fact, reference only some runs need moved to a sibling file). A script fix that adds a branch gets a small test.
5. **Test** by running the skill for real where it is safe. Data sent to an outside service (Jev, email, Teams) waits for Eric.
6. **Codex review**: `codex exec -s read-only "<prompt>" < /dev/null` on the diff (without `< /dev/null` it can wait on stdin forever), output to `~/.claude/audits/codex-review-<topic>-<date>.{md,txt}`. Check each finding before fixing it.
7. **Close**: portability check (`python3 ~/DEV/KeystoneOS/scripts/skill-portability-check.py`), commit by path in each repo touched, push, and add a line to `~/DEV/docs/STATUS.md` (and the touched repo's own STATUS).

## Done

| Date | Skill | Commits | Headline |
|---|---|---|---|
| 2026-10-25 | `closeout` | skills `740138a` (review: `~/.claude/audits/2026-10-25-closeout-skill-review.md`) | Steps in run order; done line. |
| 2026-10-25 | `claude-stack-doctor` | skills `31e7631` | Split into SKILL + FIXES + WINDOWS; false OKs fixed. |
| 2026-10-30 | `doctor-plus` | skills `ef2e377`, `be02868` | User-invoked; steps and done line; one report home. |
| 2026-10-30 | `weekly-review` | skills `db60b87`, `8e0ea63`, `fe6b76b` | No `python` on the Mac; `--agent` emptied Fireflies rows; one ask with picks. |
| 2026-10-30 | `backup` | skills `ab87c9d`, `3d15e0d`, `fe6b76b`; dotclaude `d6ab8bc`, `8fcfb93` | Stale 21:00 schedule; a dry run could hide a failed day. |
| 2026-10-30 | `meeting-sync`, `fireflies-intake` | skills `dfd95d1`, `37f93fc`, `fe6b76b`; KeystoneOS `13f7dbf`, `bf1250d` | 06:00 job exported first, so rename and Jev tag never ran. |
| 2026-10-30 | `memory-write` | skills `7a9dd89`; dotclaude `d6fa209` | Tier 0 claimed the daily log (pointer only); bench check counted hits, so a new question was never guarded. |
| 2026-10-30 | `dev-sync` | skills `be6bce0`; dotclaude `a29d6b0` | Nothing synced `claude-memory-compiler`, or `SecondBrain` on a day the backup skipped; missing nested repos cloned to the top level. |
| 2026-10-30 | `startup` | skills `908a5a4`; dotclaude `a37a767`; SportScienceResearchRepo `e34ced7` | First real run since the 10-29 rebuild: works; answered/repeated decisions kept showing (script hides only items that start with ANSWERED/RESOLVED). |

## Gotchas
- `uv run --with playwright` pulls the newest playwright. When it updates, the capture dies with `Executable doesn't exist at .../chromium-<N>`. Fix: `uv run --with playwright python -m playwright install chromium`, then re-run.

- One failed attempt per team is normal; the retry recovers it.

- CFBD dates a TBD kickoff at 00:00 UTC, the evening before in Central. `market_view.py` uses a 6-day window so next week's TBD games stay out.

content.text:
Base directory for this skill: /Users/kristinarash/.claude/skills/name-meetings

# Name Meetings

Eric does not name most Fireflies recordings, and an unnamed one exports to the vault as `2026-10-29_Oct_29_0944_AM.md`. This skill finds generic titles, proposes real ones from the AI summary, and writes the approved ones back to Fireflies, the source of truth. `scripts/rename.py` is the only write path: it verifies every write by reading the title back (the CLI and the MCP rename tools are broken; [REFERENCE.md → Why renames bypass the CLI and MCP](REFERENCE.md#why-renames-bypass-the-cli-and-mcp)).

Detail lives in [REFERENCE.md](REFERENCE.md); load only the section a step names. Below, `R=~/.claude/skills/name-meetings/scripts/rename.py`.

## Steps

1. **Auth.** `fireflies-pp-cli doctor --agent` must show `"auth": "configured"`. Otherwise stop and give Eric the fix from `pp-fireflies` → Auth Setup.

2. **Resume the ledger.** The pending-renames file is `pending_renames_file` in `~/.claude/skills/_shared/config.<platform>.json` ([REFERENCE.md → Pending-renames file](REFERENCE.md#pending-renames-file)). If `pending[]` has entries, they are already approved: say "Resuming N pending renames" and run `python3 $R --pending` (step 6 explains its output). A `STOP` here ends the writing for this run: go to step 7 if any line was `OK`, otherwise to step 8. Entries in `review[]` join the step 5 table as candidates; in Unattended mode they stay where they are.

3. **List the window.** Refresh the local DB in full, then list id, local date, title and speakers:

   ```bash
   fireflies-pp-cli sync --full --resources transcripts --agent
   fireflies-pp-cli transcripts find --from 30 --processed-only --limit 100000 --json --no-input \
     | python3 -c 'import json,sys,datetime as D
   for x in json.load(sys.stdin):
       t = D.datetime.fromisoformat(x["dateString"].replace("Z", "+00:00")).astimezone()
       print(x["id"], t.strftime("%Y-%m-%d %H:%M"), json.dumps(x["title"]), "speakers=" + ",".join(s["name"] for s in x.get("speakers") or []))'
   ```

   Change `--from` when Eric names a window ("last 60 days"); without it `find` covers all time, which is slow to rename. When meeting-sync passes ids, keep only those. The flags each fix a trap ([REFERENCE.md → CLI gotchas](REFERENCE.md#cli-gotchas)): `--full` so the list is current, `--limit 100000` past the default 100, and no `--agent`, whose compact output drops the date and speakers.

4. **Detect generics.** Match each title against [REFERENCE.md → Generic-title patterns](REFERENCE.md#generic-title-patterns). Every other title is curated and stays as it is, including Eric's `Series_MMDDYYYY` names (`StaffMeet_10222026`).

   The list can hold **ghosts**: meetings deleted from Fireflies that `sync --full` never prunes. Nothing in a read tells them apart, so keep every candidate regardless of age; the write in step 6 reports a ghost as `GONE` ([REFERENCE.md → Deleted transcripts](REFERENCE.md#deleted-transcripts-linger-in-the-local-db)).

5. **Propose, then approve.** For each candidate read the summary first:

   ```bash
   fireflies-pp-cli summary <id> --format gist --json --agent
   ```

   Build the title from the gist, keywords, overview and the step 3 speakers, by [REFERENCE.md → Title construction rules](REFERENCE.md#title-construction-rules). A meeting in one of Eric's recurring series takes the series name; a gist too vague to name gets `[skip — gist too vague]`, for Eric to name in the Fireflies UI. When several candidates come from one event, ask Eric what the event was and offer a shared prefix.

   Show a table `# | Date | Current | Proposed | Action` (`✓` apply, `—` skip), then `AskUserQuestion` "How should I apply these renames?" with **Approve all / Edit rows / Apply subset / Cancel**. Edit rows: ask which rows and what titles, then confirm the revised table. Apply subset: ask which rows ("1,3,5", "skip 2,4"). Cancel: end the run with nothing applied.

6. **Apply.** Add each approved row to `pending[]` as `{"id": "<meetingId>", "title": "<title>"}`, keeping what the file already holds and removing any `review[]` entry for that id, then run `python3 $R --pending`. It spaces the writes, verifies each by read-back and rewrites the file. Read its lines, never just the exit code:
   - `OK` verified; gone from `pending[]`.
   - `FAIL` transient (timeout, 5xx, read-back mismatch); stays in `pending[]` for the next run.
   - `GONE` permanent (`Transcript not found`, a title under 5 or over 256 characters, a malformed entry); dropped. Report it as unrenamable, with the reason.
   - `STOP` rate limited; the rest stay in `pending[]`. Make no more writes this run; step 7 still verifies the `OK` ones.

   When both arrays are empty afterwards, delete the file.

7. **Wait, re-sync, verify.** Fireflies' list endpoint (what `sync` and `find` read) lags the single-transcript endpoint `rename.py` verifies against by minutes. Run `sleep 270` as a background Bash job, then `fireflies-pp-cli sync --full --resources transcripts --agent` and the step 3 list again, and confirm each new title. A title still old after the wait means more lag: wait and re-sync once more. The rename already verified, so the fix is waiting; a second rename can clobber a good title.
   - A plain `sync` (no `--full`) never picks up title edits yet exits 0 with `total: 0`; the re-run list is the proof.
   - If the sync fails twice, the renames still stand in Fireflies; only the local DB is stale. Say so and give the command: `fireflies-pp-cli sync --full --resources transcripts --agent`.
   - Generics you never proposed mean the step 3 DB was stale: name them and offer a second pass.
   - A renamed meeting already in the vault (its id is in meeting-sync's `.sync-state.json`) keeps its generic filename; re-export makes a second file. Name it in the report and point to meeting-sync's filename drift audit (`DRIFT.md`).

8. **Report**, 3–5 lines: N scanned / M generic · K applied · F left in `pending[]` (next run resumes) · G gone · S skipped for manual naming · re-sync status (verified, or the stale-DB warning) · vault files left with a generic name.

**Done when** every generic title in the window is verified renamed in the step 7 list, queued in `pending[]` or `review[]`, or named in the report as skipped or gone, and the report says whether the local DB matches Fireflies.

## Unattended mode

Only when the calling skill declares it (meeting-sync does, in its step 2, scoped to the ids it passes). Every step runs as above, summaries and proposals included; only step 5's approval table and question are replaced, by the confidence gate in [REFERENCE.md → Unattended mode](REFERENCE.md#unattended-mode): rows that pass go to `pending[]` and are applied; every other row is appended to `review[]` for Eric's next interactive run. With no generic titles among the ids, return to the caller with nothing to report. This is the only path that renames without Eric's approval.

class TestUndoSafety(ServerCase):
    """The undo snapshot can be hours old. Restoring it blind would silently erase
    anything the CLI or the `project` skill wrote in the meantime — including
    `ideas`, which this page does not render at all, so the loss would be invisible.
    """

    def registry(self):
        return json.loads(self.get("/api/registry").read())

    def external_write(self):
        """Stand-in for `portfolio.py add-idea` running in a terminal."""
        path = self.dir / "portfolio.json"
        data = portfolio.load_registry(path)
        portfolio.add_idea(data, "an idea captured outside the board")
        portfolio.save_registry(path, data)

    def refused_undo(self):
        self.post("/api/project/A", {"status": "paused"})
        self.external_write()
        with self.assertRaises(urllib.error.HTTPError) as cm:
            self.post("/api/undo", {})
        return cm.exception

    def test_undo_after_an_external_write_returns_409(self):
        exc = self.refused_undo()
        self.assertEqual(exc.code, 409)
        self.assertIn("outside the board", json.loads(exc.read())["error"])
        exc.close()

    def test_the_external_write_survives_a_refused_undo(self):
        self.refused_undo().close()
        data = self.registry()
        self.assertEqual(len(data["ideas"]), 1)                     # not destroyed
        self.assertEqual(data["projects"][0]["status"], "paused")   # board write kept

    def test_a_refused_undo_clears_the_buffer(self):
        self.refused_undo().close()
        with self.assertRaises(urllib.error.HTTPError) as cm:
            self.post("/api/undo", {})

def idea_name(data: dict, pitch: str, name: str | None = None) -> str:
    """A unique `[A-Za-z0-9_]` name for a new inbox card.

    Unique across inbox[] and projects[]: board_ops finds inbox records by name,
    so a twin would make promote/archive/delete act on the wrong card. The name
    also becomes the dev_folder on promotion, hence the narrow character set.
    """
    base = re.sub(r"[^A-Za-z0-9]+", "_", name or "").strip("_")
    if not base:
        words = re.findall(r"[A-Za-z0-9]+", pitch)[:4]
        base = "_".join(w[:1].upper() + w[1:] for w in words) or "Idea"
    taken = {r.get("name") for r in data.get("inbox", [])} | {p.get("name") for p in data.get("projects", [])}
    candidate, n = base, 2
    while candidate in taken:
        candidate, n = f"{base}_{n}", n + 1
    return candidate


def add_idea(data: dict, pitch: str, source: str = "", name: str | None = None) -> dict:
    """Capture an idea as an inbox card, the list the board shows (2026-10-31).

    It used to append to `ideas[]`, which the board never renders, so captured
    ideas were invisible there. `ideas[]` stays as history.
    """
    if not pitch.strip():
        raise RegistryError("idea pitch is empty")
    card_name = idea_name(data, pitch, name)
    record = {
        "name": card_name,
        "dev_folder": card_name,
        "source": source,
        "status": "paused",
        "purpose": pitch.strip(),
        "captured_at": _dt.datetime.now().isoformat(timespec="seconds"),
    }

        with self.assertRaises(portfolio.RegistryError):
            portfolio.add_idea({"meta": {}, "ideas": [], "projects": []}, "   ")

EOF
```

## Ideas live off the board

`add-idea` appends to the registry's `ideas` list. The board shows projects and its own
`inbox` list; `ideas` appear only in chat. The N in `idea captured (<N> in inbox)` counts
ideas with `status: inbox`, not the board's Inbox column. So after capturing an idea, say it
is in the ideas list (N waiting) and that `/project promote <idea>` puts it on the board.

## Verbs

**Name matching** (every verb that takes `<name>`): read `portfolio.json` and match the name
against `projects[].name`. One clear match: use that exact name. Several or none: ask Eric
which project before running anything.

### `idea <pitch>`
`add-idea "<pitch>" --source "<where it came from, ≤8 words>"`, e.g. `--source "chat about
GPS vendor gaps"` (a place, not just "chat").

### `update <name> <note>`
`add-update "<name>" "<note>"`, plus `--next-action "<step>"` when Eric gave one.

### `start` / `park` / `done <name>`
`set-status "<name>" active|paused|done`, with `--note` when Eric gave a reason. Starting a
`job`, `side` or `tool` row with no `receiver`: ask Eric who it is for, then run
`set-receiver` with his words (`me: <why>` when it is for himself).

### `stage <name> <stage>`
`set-stage "<name>" "<stage>"`. When the stage is `shipped`, offer once: "Want me to run
/harvest on <name> to distill it into your SecondBrain and log the shipped artifact?" On
yes, invoke the `harvest` skill for that project.

### `promote <idea>` and `rank`
Both change the registry where no CLI command reaches: follow
[`REGISTRY-EDITS.md`](REGISTRY-EDITS.md). Dragging cards on the board re-ranks faster.

### bare `/project`
Run `board.py --background` and give the URL. Then list the `ideas` with
`status: inbox` (first ~80 characters of each pitch), since the board does not show them.

## After a change

The board picks up registry changes on its next poll (a few seconds); there is nothing to
render. Tell Eric in one line what changed. Closeout commits the registry as
`data: board edits <date>`, so leave `portfolio.json` uncommitted unless Eric asks.

Delete a project or idea only after Eric confirms that exact row.

# /project: portfolio registry

Drives the `project-triage` CLI. The registry, `portfolio.json`, is the single
source of truth; each repo's `docs/STATUS.md` holds its tasks, which the board
reads only.

## Paths

- `$PT` is the folder holding `portfolio_json` in `~/.claude/skills/_shared/config.<platform>.json`.
  On the Mac that is `~/DEV/project-triage`: start each Bash call with
  `PT=~/DEV/project-triage` (the shell does not keep it between calls).
- Interpreter: `python3` on the Mac (there is no `python`). On Windows, use `python` and the
  `portfolio_json` folder from `config.windows.json` wherever this skill says `python3` and `$PT`.
- `portfolio.py` makes every change and always writes the live `$PT/portfolio.json` (only
  `slate-check` and the read commands take `--registry`). `board.py` serves the board.

## CLI

```
python3 "$PT/portfolio.py" add-idea "<pitch>" --source "<source>"
python3 "$PT/portfolio.py" add-update "<name>" "<note>" [--next-action "<step>"]
python3 "$PT/portfolio.py" set-stage "<name>" "<stage>"
python3 "$PT/portfolio.py" set-status "<name>" active|paused|done [--note "<note>"]
python3 "$PT/portfolio.py" set-receiver "<name>" "<who, or me: why>"
python3 "$PT/board.py" --background
```

|---|---|
| `add-idea` | `idea captured (<N> in inbox)` |
| `add-update` | `updated <name>` |
| `set-stage` | `stage set: <name> → <stage>` |
| `set-status` | `status set: <name> → <status>` |
| `set-receiver` | `<Name>: receiver <who>` |
| `board.py --background` | `board started at <url>` or `board already running at <url>` |

  Stages, in ladder order: `idea grilled spec planned building shipped`.
- `set-status active` on a row that was not active stamps `started` and renumbers the lane.
- A refused change prints `[error] <msg>` to stderr, exits 2 and leaves `portfolio.json`
  unchanged; a bad argument prints argparse usage and also exits 2. `board.py` prints

# Registry edits with no CLI command

`promote` and `rank` change `portfolio.json` through `portfolio.load_registry` /
`save_registry`, run from `$PT` (see SKILL.md, Paths). Use these functions, not the Edit
tool: `save_registry` validates the whole file first, refreshes `portfolio.json.bak` the
way the CLI and the board do (the provenance check in Tier A memory reads it), and
replaces the file atomically while the board polls it. Load, change and save in one
script, as below, so a board edit has well under a second to land in between.

A refused save raises `RegistryError: <problems>` and leaves the file unchanged: show it
verbatim and stop.

## promote `<idea>`

1. Find the idea: `ideas[]` rows with `status: inbox` whose `pitch` matches. One match, or
   ask Eric which.
2. Check `projects[]` for a row that already carries this idea (another session may have
   added it). If one exists, only set the idea's `status` to `promoted` and say so.
3. Ask Eric for the lane (`job`, `side`, `system`, `knowledge`, `tool`), the project name
   (`Words_With_Underscores`, matching the DEV folder when there is one), and the next
   action. Take `purpose` as one line from the pitch.

   the row its rank in the lane. The `&&` runs the start only after a clean save; if the
   start then fails, the row stays paused: show the error and stop.

```

## rank

The board shows each lane as stage columns (an `unstaged` column, then `idea` → `shipped`),
and `rank` orders the cards within a column. Board drags and card edits renumber the lane
stage by stage. So a rank order holds only within a stage.

1. Show the lane's active rows grouped by stage, in current `rank` order, and ask Eric for
   his order. If his order crosses stages, tell him the stage grouping wins.
2. Apply exactly his order: his rows take temporary ranks below 1 in that order, then the
   board's own renumbering (`_renumber`, which also numbers the lane's paused rows) gives
   every row its final rank:

```

from pathlib import Path
import portfolio as pf, board_ops
p = Path("portfolio.json"); d = pf.load_registry(p)
lane, order = "<lane>", ["<Name1>", "<Name2>"]   # Eric's order: active or paused rows only
for i, name in enumerate(order):
    row = board_ops.find(d, name)
    assert row["lane"] == lane and row["status"] in ("active", "paused"), name
    row["rank"] = i - len(order)                  # temporary; renumbered next line
board_ops._renumber(d, lane)
pf.save_registry(p, d)
print([(x["name"], x["rank"], x.get("stage")) for x in board_ops.live(d, lane) if x["status"] == "active"])
EOF
```

# Skill audit list

"The list" for skill audits. When Eric says "audit the next skill on the list", take the first row under **Next** and follow **Method**.

**Rules (Eric, 2026-10-30):**

- **Next always holds five.** When a skill's audit is done, in the same commit as the fix: move its row to **Done** (date, commits, headline), then refill **Next** with the top skill from `python3 ~/.claude/scripts/skill-audit-next.py` as the new last row (runs, why, care).
- **Done is final.** A skill in **Done** never returns to **Next**, unless Eric explicitly names it to be added back. Then move its row back to **Next** and note the date he asked. The script already skips every skill in either table.
- **Every audit runs `mattpocock-skills:writing-for-agents`.** Call it through the Skill tool at the start of each audit, and again for the review pass, even when it ran earlier in the session. Working from memory of it is the slip this rule exists for (the 10-30 meeting-sync audit missed six wording faults until the skill was called).
- **Audit agents run on Sonnet (Eric, 2026-10-31).** When audits run as subagents, pass `model: "sonnet"`. Never Haiku. Parallel agents each edit only their own skill, commit by path, and never push; the main session updates this file and pushes once at the end.

## Next

Ranked by real use: Skill-tool calls and typed `/commands` in the last 60 days of session logs, owned skills only (`skill-audit-next.py`). First five picked 2026-10-30; this five picked 2026-10-31.

| # | Skill | Runs (60 d) | Why it is on the list | Care |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | `new-project` | 2 | Scaffolds a DEV project: repo, AGENTS.md, STATUS, private GitHub repo. | Creating a GitHub repo is outside-facing: test in a temp folder with no remote; a real repo waits for Eric. |

Eric's local runner patch forces `gpt-6-astra` at low effort and breaks one unit test (10-31 codex-review audit). |
| 5 | `codex-build` | 1 | Codex builds a work order; Claude inspects the changes. | Same vendored repo as `claudex-loop`: commit locally, never push. |

When the script prints nothing, every used skill has been audited: tell Eric, and keep **Next** shorter than five.

## Method

What "audit like we've been doing" means, in order:

1. **Load** `mattpocock-skills:writing-for-agents` through the Skill tool (see Rules).
2. **Read** the skill, its other files, and the scripts and CLIs it calls. Find its callers (`grep -rn '<name>' ~/.claude/skills/*/SKILL.md`) and any scheduled job that does the same work.
3. **Verify every claim** against the real thing: paths exist, `--help` matches the flags, error codes and log lines exist in the script, the schedule matches the plist. Look at recent real runs (logs, outputs) for what actually went wrong.
4. **Fix**: real bugs first, then the writing-for-agents pass (steps in run order, a **Done when** line, positive rules, one home per fact, reference only some runs need moved to a sibling file). A script fix that adds a branch gets a small test.
5. **Test** by running the skill for real where it is safe. Data sent to an outside service (Jev, email, Teams) waits for Eric.
6. **Codex review**: `codex exec -s read-only "<prompt>" < /dev/null` on the diff (without `< /dev/null` it can wait on stdin forever), output to `~/.claude/audits/codex-review-<topic>-<date>.{md,txt}`. Check each finding before fixing it.
7. **Close**: portability check (`python3 ~/DEV/KeystoneOS/scripts/skill-portability-check.py`), commit by path in each repo touched, push, and add a line to `~/DEV/docs/STATUS.md` (and the touched repo's own STATUS).

# Skill audit list

"The list" for skill audits. When Eric says "audit the next skill on the list", take the first row under **Next** and follow **Method**.

**Rules (Eric, 2026-10-30):**

- **Next always holds five.** When a skill's audit is done, in the same commit as the fix: move its row to **Done** (date, commits, headline), then refill **Next** with the top skill from `python3 ~/.claude/scripts/skill-audit-next.py` as the new last row (runs, why, care).
- **Done is final.** A skill in **Done** never returns to **Next**, unless Eric explicitly names it to be added back. Then move its row back to **Next** and note the date he asked. The script already skips every skill in either table.
- **Every audit runs `mattpocock-skills:writing-for-agents`.** Call it through the Skill tool at the start of each audit, and again for the review pass, even when it ran earlier in the session. Working from memory of it is the slip this rule exists for (the 10-30 meeting-sync audit missed six wording faults until the skill was called).
- **Audit agents run on Sonnet (Eric, 2026-10-31).** When audits run as subagents, pass `model: "sonnet"`. Never Haiku. Parallel agents each edit only their own skill, commit by path, and never push; the main session updates this file and pushes once at the end.

## Next

Ranked by real use: Skill-tool calls and typed `/commands` in the last 60 days of session logs, owned skills only (`skill-audit-next.py`). First five picked 2026-10-30; this five picked 2026-10-31.

| # | Skill | Runs (60 d) | Why it is on the list | Care |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | `new-project` | 2 | Scaffolds a DEV project: repo, AGENTS.md, STATUS, private GitHub repo. | Creating a GitHub repo is outside-facing: test in a temp folder with no remote; a real repo waits for Eric. |
| 2 | `session-miner` | 2 | Mines recent sessions for uncaptured lessons and routes them to memory, vault or a skill. | Writes memory and vault notes: test with output to a temp folder; session logs may hold secrets (Tier A `session-history-tracked`). |
| 3 | `sports-science-research-grounding` | 2 | Zotero-first answers to sport-science questions; batch full-library runs. | Full-library batch is costly: test one question, never a batch unasked. |

## Method

What "audit like we've been doing" means, in order:
